clinicalPearls: Subacute (days to a few weeks) behavioral change, memory decline, psychiatric symptoms, seizures, or movement disorder should prompt consideration of autoimmune encephalitis, especially in young adults or children.

Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis classically evolves through a viral-like prodrome, then psychiatric/behavioral disturbance, followed by seizures, movement disorder (orofacial dyskinesias), autonomic instability, and decreased consciousness.
Faciobrachial dystonic seizures are a highly characteristic, near-pathognomonic sign of anti-LGI1 encephalitis and often precede overt cognitive decline.
Always search for an underlying tumor (ovarian teratoma in anti-NMDAR disease, thymoma, small-cell lung cancer) since paraneoplastic triggers are common and tumor removal aids recovery.
MRI can be normal or show only subtle mesial temporal T2/FLAIR signal change; a normal scan does not exclude the diagnosis.
CSF often shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and oligoclonal bands; antibody testing should be sent on both serum and CSF since CSF sensitivity is higher for some antibodies (e.g., NMDAR).
Response to immunotherapy can be slow (weeks to months), and early aggressive treatment plus tumor removal improves long-term outcome.
Relapses occur in a meaningful proportion of patients, particularly with anti-NMDAR encephalitis, warranting longitudinal follow-up.
harrison.pathophysiology: Autoimmune encephalitis results from antibody-mediated or T-cell-mediated attack on neuronal surface or intracellular antigens, producing limbic or diffuse cortical dysfunction. Surface-antigen antibodies (e.g., against the NMDA receptor, LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B receptor) directly disrupt synaptic receptor function and are often reversible with immunotherapy, whereas antibodies against intracellular (onconeural) antigens reflect cytotoxic T-cell-mediated neuronal injury and are less responsive to treatment. A subset is paraneoplastic, triggered by tumor expression of neuronal antigens (e.g., ovarian teratoma expressing NMDA receptors), while others arise post-infection (e.g., following herpes simplex encephalitis) or without any identifiable trigger.
additionalDifferentials: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and other rapidly progressive dementias
Non-convulsive status epilepticus of other etiology
nonInfectiousMimics: Primary psychiatric illness (schizophreniform psychosis, catatonia, bipolar disorder)
Non-convulsive status epilepticus from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Serum and CSF autoimmune/paraneoplastic antibody panel (NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA, and onconeural antibodies) — confirms specific antibody-mediated syndrome
MRI brain with contrast — assesses for mesial temporal/limbic T2-FLAIR signal change and excludes structural or infectious mimics
CSF analysis (cell count, protein, oligoclonal bands, HSV PCR) — distinguishes autoimmune from infectious causes and supports diagnosis
EEG — detects epileptiform activity, extreme delta brush pattern (suggestive of anti-NMDAR encephalitis), or non-convulsive status epilepticus
Whole-body imaging (CT/MRI chest-abdomen-pelvis, pelvic ultrasound/MRI in women, testicular ultrasound in men) — screens for occult tumor, especially ovarian teratoma or thymoma
FDG-PET brain — may show characteristic regional hyper- or hypometabolism when MRI is unrevealing
Thyroid function and thyroid antibodies — evaluates for Hashimoto encephalopathy as a mimic
Tumor markers/gynecologic evaluation as guided by antibody subtype — directs targeted tumor search
redFlags: Rapid decline in consciousness, autonomic instability (labile blood pressure, arrhythmia, central hypoventilation) requiring ICU-level monitoring
Faciobrachial dystonic seizures with rapidly progressive cognitive decline (LGI1 encephalitis)
New psychiatric presentation in a young woman with subsequent neurologic signs — evaluate urgently for ovarian teratoma and anti-NMDAR encephalitis
Failure to improve or worsening despite first-line immunotherapy — consider escalation and repeat tumor search
Signs suggesting an alternative treatable infectious cause (fever, meningismus) that must be excluded/treated empirically first
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing early psychiatric or behavioral presentations as a primary psychiatric disorder, delaying immunotherapy
Excluding the diagnosis because MRI or initial antibody testing is negative — antibody testing can be falsely negative early, and CSF testing may be more sensitive than serum
Failing to empirically treat for herpes simplex encephalitis while autoimmune work-up is pending
Overlooking the need for repeated or interval tumor screening, since a causative tumor may not be apparent at initial presentation
harrison.prognosis: Many patients, particularly those with anti-NMDAR or anti-LGI1 encephalitis, achieve substantial or full recovery with prompt immunotherapy and tumor removal when applicable, though recovery may take many months and some residual cognitive or behavioral deficits can persist. Relapses occur in a meaningful minority, and outcomes are generally worse with delayed treatment, intracellular (onconeural) antibody syndromes, or need for prolonged intensive care.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Autoimmune and Paraneoplastic Encephalitis (Nervous System Disorders section)
management: First-line immunotherapy with corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin and/or plasma exchange.
Second-line immunotherapy with rituximab or cyclophosphamide for treatment-refractory disease.
Search for and removal of an associated tumour, particularly ovarian teratoma in anti-NMDA-receptor disease, which aids recovery.
Symptomatic management with antiseizure medication, control of dyskinesias and psychiatric symptoms, and intensive-care support for autonomic instability and reduced consciousness.
Monitoring for relapse and periodic repeat tumour screening after recovery.
Multidisciplinary neurology, oncology, psychiatry and intensive-care management, with early escalation for status epilepticus or autonomic and respiratory compromise.
